item.title: Quantum Knowledge Distillation: State-of-the-art, Applications and Open Problems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article provides the first systematic map of how knowledge‑distillation techniques can be leveraged across quantum and classical machine‑learning models, highlighting both compression gains and more ambitious cross‑architecture transfers such as circuit approximation and distributed training. By juxtaposing teacher–student configurations with the specific quantum resources used—ranging from raw measurement probabilities to full‑circuit objectives—it clarifies where genuine quantum advantage has been demonstrated versus where results remain marginal or hardware‑limited. The survey’s critical assessment of experimental evidence and its call for standardized reporting give researchers a concrete roadmap for turning these promising ideas into reproducible, scalable applications.

Knowledge distillation transfers predictions, representations, or other supervisory information between learning models and is increasingly investigated in quantum machine learning. Its applications extend beyond compression to cross-architecture transfer, circuit approximation, distributed learning, and classical deployment of models trained using quantum-derived supervision. This survey reviews these approaches using two complementary classification axes: teacher-student configuration and the role of quantum resources in the distillation process. Quantum-inspired methods are discussed separately from methods that simulate quantum computations classically or execute them on quantum hardware. We explain how measurement probabilities, expectation values, classical readouts, state overlaps, and circuit-level objectives support different transfer mechanisms. We then critically assess the presented results against baseline design, execution conditions, uncertainty, and resource costs. The evidence shows that distillation can improve selected quantum students, but benefits are task- and architecture-dependent, and several studies find negligible gains or even performance degradation. Evaluations on physical quantum hardware remain limited, with some testing individual quantum components rather than complete learning pipelines. Heterogeneous protocols and incomplete resource reporting prevent general conclusions about practical quantum advantage. We identify priorities for controlled benchmarking, noise-aware learning, reproducible evaluation, and efficient transfer between quantum and classical models.

item.title: Room-Temperature Quantum Emission from Boron Nitride Nanotubes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that boron‑nitride nanotubes can host bright, room‑temperature single‑photon emitters across the visible spectrum with lifetimes as short as 0.5 ns—roughly twice as fast as the best hBN flakes reported to date. By packing multiple spectrally distinct emitters along a ~25 nm‑diameter tube and demonstrating that surface coating suppresses blinking, the work offers a compact, multi‑wavelength source that can be positioned deterministically in photonic circuits, addressing a long‑standing bottleneck for scalable quantum key distribution hardware. The results complement recent advances in 2D hBN emitters while sidestepping their integration challenges, though further work will be needed to verify long‑term stability and coupling efficiency in realistic device architectures.

Quantum information systems such as quantum key distribution and quantum communications require bright, high-purity, stable sources of single photons to act as carriers of quantum information. As such, methods for obtaining single photon emitters (SPEs) in solid-state devices capable of articulating with quantum photonic circuits are a necessary obstacle that must be overcome. Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) flakes have been extensively studied as a host material for SPEs, though working in two dimensions is accompanied by engineering complexity. However, dimensionality can be reduced through the implementation of boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs). Here we investigate the potential of BNNTs as room-temperature SPEs using confocal photoluminescence microscopy and Hanbury Brown-Twiss interferometry. Quantum emitters were found in BNNTs spanning the entirety of the visible spectrum, including spectral regions where SPEs within hBN have not been reported. Furthermore, each tube was found to possess multiple SPEs at varying emission wavelengths along the length, exhibiting lifetimes as fast as 0.5 ns, which is about two-fold faster than the fastest hBN SPEs. Additionally, we demonstrate that surface passivation/coating mitigates blinking events, therefore increasing the emitter stability. Thus, BNNTs can function as a single structure supporting a variety of multiwavelength SPE sources, while maintaining a compact radius of ~25 nm, making them ideally suited for deterministic placement and integration within nanophotonic devices such as waveguides and interferometric filters.

item.title: Recovery gates as a resource in repetition-code process tomography: exhaustive gate-optimal designs for three, five and seven qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the number of physical Pauli recovery gates needed for repetition‑code process tomography can be dramatically reduced—down to zero for three qubits and just five for seven—by exhaustively searching optimal decoder designs rather than relying on the conventional minimum‑weight rule. The resulting gate‑optimal decoders deliver up to an order‑of‑magnitude improvement in tomographic precision while cutting experimental runtime, a benefit that directly supports current efforts to benchmark and calibrate noisy intermediate‑scale quantum processors more efficiently. However, the advantage diminishes for larger codes where full decoding can even lose rank, underscoring that scaling these techniques will require careful conditioning of hardware and possibly new decoder heuristics.

Process tomography built on stabilizer codes compares the logical channel of a repetition code with a reference channel, and the decoder that produces that channel is almost always fixed to the standard minimum-weight one. We ask how many physical single-qubit Pauli gates the decoder actually needs when the measurement basis is fixed---the constraint under which the count is a resource rather than a bookkeeping artefact. Exhaustive enumeration of every recovery design for $n=3$, $5$ and $7$ qubits, with rank decided by exact modular arithmetic at two primes, gives minimal counts of $0$, $1$ and $5$ gates, against $6$, $10$ and $14$ for first-order decoding and $6$, $50$ and $308$ for full minimum-weight decoding. The count depends only on how many sites are corrected and never on which, so the two halves of the design problem separate. Correcting more sites is not monotonically better: at $n=7$ full decoding loses three dimensions of rank, and under a calibration-residual floor the precision curve at $n=3$ is U-shaped. The three-gate design is $9.5$ times more precise than the standard six-gate decoder at the median of $40$ sampled working points, and more precise at every one of them ($1.8$ to $88$ times); the size of that factor belongs to the working point, the ordering does not. Reaching a $10$\,mrad rms error then costs $1.2\times10^{7}$ shots in $65$\,s on a current superconducting device at a well-conditioned point, while $n\ge5$ stays out of reach for conditioning reasons rather than gate-count reasons. Finally, the optimal designs are not covariant under chain reversal: they separate the mirror pair of arXiv:2610.19779 by $1.3\times10^{-3}$ while leaving the Jacobian at full rank.

item.title: Beyond Quantum Messages: Toward Quantum-Native Network Functioning
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pushes the quantum‑internet vision beyond merely ferrying qubits, arguing that core network functions themselves can be built on quantum phenomena such as entanglement superposition and non‑local connectivity. By treating entanglement as a stateful, visible resource, it opens a design space for truly “quantum‑native” routing, addressing and topology that could cut overhead and enable new distributed algorithms. The proposal dovetails with recent efforts to embed entanglement‑based primitives into networking stacks, signaling a shift toward infrastructure where the network’s logic is intrinsically quantum. Practical impact will hinge on overcoming decoherence and demonstrating these concepts on real hardware.

The Quantum Internet is commonly envisioned as a network that transports quantum states and distributes entanglement as the key resource underpinning distributed quantum applications. This view is necessary but incomplete if quantum phenomena are confined to what the network carries or manages, while network functionalities remain grounded predominantly in classical abstractions. This Perspective advances a broader thesis: quantum phenomena can also participate directly in the realization of network functionalities. We first establish the architectural baseline by introducing entanglement as a stateful network resource whose operational condition is non-locally distributed across remote nodes, evolves through manipulation or consumption, and degrades over time through decoherence. Its evolving state must therefore remain visible to the functionalities acting on it. We then move beyond resource visibility and use two mechanisms as proof points of a broader quantum-native functional design space: entanglement generation during propagation through coherent spatial-path superposition, and operational connectivity induced by shared entanglement that can depart from the physical graph. These examples show that paths, neighbors, or participating nodes may become operationally relevant in ways determined by quantum coherence and shared entanglement, rather than by physical connectivity alone. We identify Quantum Addressing as a transversal abstraction capable of representing such relations while complementing, rather than replacing, classical addressing and signaling. The resulting perspective broadens the Quantum Internet from transporting quantum information and distributing entanglement to exploiting quantum phenomena in network functioning, opening a coupled frontier spanning routing, forwarding, control, and functionality placement.

item.title: Certifying quantum code and circuit distances at scale
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first scalable technique for rigorously certifying quantum code and circuit distances, turning previously heuristic upper‑bounds into provable exact values even for codes as large as 31 200 qubits and memory circuits with hundreds of thousands of fault mechanisms. By exposing overestimated distances in ten recent papers and showing how schedule tweaks can recover lost error‑suppression on IBM’s two‑gross memory blocks, the work directly sharpens resource estimates and helps hardware teams decide which partially defective chips remain usable. The ability to certify true distance at this scale is a crucial step toward reliable fault‑tolerant architectures, though the dynamic‑programming approach still demands substantial classical compute power for the biggest instances.

Code and circuit distances characterize how strongly quantum error correction suppresses logical errors and guide code comparisons, schedule choices and resource estimates. Yet many published distances are only upper bounds from heuristic searches. Here, we express both distances as tropical partition functions and evaluate them with rank-based dynamic programming and weight-bounded search. Circuit reductions and relaxations shrink the problems, and proved lower bounds with explicit logical errors of matching weight certify exact values. On two benchmarks, our method certifies more instances than all other tested exact solvers combined. We certify distances for codes with up to 31,200 qubits, such as Google's modular hyperbolic codes, and for memory circuits with up to $8\times10^5$ fault mechanisms, such as those of high-rate Cornucopia codes. Our audit of 26 recent papers identifies overestimated distances and non-tight upper bounds in 10 papers, with a maximum discrepancy of at least eight. Certified distances also guide circuit design and show which defective chips remain usable. In particular, we certify circuit distance 16 for IBM's two-gross memory circuits with the standard schedule, not the assumed 18, whereas redesigned schedules reach 18 at one noisy cycle, at the cost of one more timestep per cycle. At 99.98% junction yield, keeping gross-code memory blocks with dead checks that are certified at distance 10 or more raises the estimated usable share from 53% for perfect blocks alone to 94% with an improved schedule.

item.title: Optimal finite-copy readout of three-qubit entanglement with state retention
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints the exact resource‑trade‑off for certifying genuine three‑qubit GHZ entanglement while still preserving the original state, showing that five copies already boost the success probability and enable conditional state retention—a capability that could streamline error‑diagnostics in near‑term quantum processors. By framing the problem in terms of symmetry‑based “additional‑copy” theorems and delivering concrete local Schur measurement circuits, it connects abstract entanglement theory to hardware‑friendly protocols that are directly implementable on superconducting or trapped‑ion platforms. The results also clarify how multi‑copy strategies outperform binary thinning for variance reduction, offering a practical blueprint for more efficient quantum sensing and verification tasks as devices scale beyond a few qubits.

For unknown three-qubit pure states, we characterize the optimal trade-off among GHZ-class certification, binary probability readout of the three-tangle, and conditional state retention. The vanishing ideal of the null class specifies the optimal certification subspace, while a polynomial multiplication operator gives the spectral limit for binary readout. Four copies are necessary for a nonzero certificate. A fifth copy raises the optimal success probability from $τ^{2}/48$ to $5τ^{2}/72$ and permits the original unknown state to be retained, where $τ$ is the three-tangle. We obtain this gain as an instance of a general symmetry-based additional-copy theorem. At six copies the optimal certification probability is $(39+2S)τ^{2}/296$, with $S=\sum_{X}\mathrm{Tr}\,ρ_{X}^{2}$, whereas the largest exact binary probability is $τ^{2}/8$. Local Schur measurements and conditional local operations with classical communication attain these bounds. Retaining the full six-copy branch record yields a weighted estimator with lower variance than binary thinning of the same data. Explicit circuits and fixed-budget comparisons connect the success probabilities to input-copy consumption, retained quantum output, and coherent gate cost.

item.title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces QDiff, a differential‑testing framework that tackles the long‑standing challenge of reliably validating quantum software stacks despite their probabilistic outputs and opaque hardware specifications. By automatically generating semantics‑preserving program variants and pre‑filtering circuits based on depth, two‑qubit gate count, error rates and T1 times, it lets developers catch bugs before expensive runs on real devices. The extensible equivalence checker—using Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests and cross‑entropy metrics—provides a statistically sound way to compare output distributions across compilers, simulators and controllers. While the approach dramatically speeds up testing and improves confidence in emerging QSS toolchains, its reliance on statistical similarity means rare but critical errors could still slip through without deeper analysis.

Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. item.title: Primitive Quantum Gates for an $SU(3)$ Discrete Subgroup: $Σ(216\times3)$
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first explicit primitive gate set for digitally simulating the 648‑element discrete subgroup of SU(3), a key building block for non‑Abelian lattice gauge theories such as QCD, and it supplies concrete qubit and qutrit–qubit decompositions for each operation. By providing detailed fault‑tolerant resource estimates—on the order of 10¹⁰ T gates for a pure‑qubit implementation and up to 10¹² R gates for a hybrid qutrit architecture—it benchmarks how far current error‑corrected hardware must progress before realistic shear‑viscosity calculations become feasible. The work therefore bridges recent algorithmic advances in quantum gauge simulations with the practical engineering challenges of scaling up fault‑tolerant quantum processors, highlighting both a clear pathway and the substantial overhead that remains.

We construct a primitive gate set for the digital quantum simulation of the $648$-element discrete subgroup of $SU(3)$, $\dsb$. The five algorithmic primitives are the inversion, group multiplication, trace, group Fourier transform, and kinetic-phase gates, for which we provide qubit and qutrit--qubit decompositions. For a fiducial shear-viscosity calculation on a $10^3$ spatial lattice with $50$ time steps and a total synthesis-error budget of $10^{-8}$, the estimated fault-tolerant costs are $2.3$--$6.8\times10^{10}$ $T$ gates in the qubit architecture and $1.3$--$5.9\times10^{12}$ $R$ gates in the qutrit--qubit architecture.

item.title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article extends the out‑of‑time‑order correlator—a key diagnostic of quantum scrambling—to systems that include local measurements and other non‑unitary processes, showing analytically how measurement rates reshape the decay of chaos signals. By confirming the theory on Quantinuum’s trapped‑ion processor despite realistic hardware noise, it provides a concrete benchmark for how decoherence and measurement back‑action alter many‑body dynamics, a topic that has surged alongside studies of measurement‑induced phase transitions. The results give quantum engineers a quantitative tool to assess and mitigate noise‑driven scrambling in near‑term simulators and sensing platforms.

We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.

item.title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that machine‑learning models can compress the raw measurement data from a quantum processor into compact representations that feed directly into classical quantum Monte Carlo, cutting the post‑processing cost by orders of magnitude and pushing chemically accurate simulations to roughly 40 qubits—more than double the previous record. By turning expensive, repeated state tomography into a reusable surrogate, the work bridges a long‑standing bottleneck in hybrid quantum‑classical workflows and promises faster, larger‑scale studies of strongly correlated materials even before fault‑tolerant hardware arrives. The results also suggest that similar data‑compression strategies could become standard tools for any algorithm that must repeatedly extract wavefunction information from noisy near‑term devices.

Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

item.title: Semi-Analytical Geometric Synthesis of Robust Quantum Controls
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that high‑fidelity gates can be engineered in milliseconds instead of minutes by turning the control problem into a geometric curve‑design task, dramatically speeding up the synthesis of dynamically corrected gates. By leveraging the Space Curve Quantum Control formalism and Pontryagin’s Maximum Principle, the authors produce smooth pulses that are simultaneously robust to amplitude drift and dephasing—an advance that could accelerate calibration cycles on noisy intermediate‑scale devices. The semi‑analytical approach bridges the gap between fully numerical optimal‑control methods and analytic pulse families, offering a practical pathway for building larger libraries of error‑resilient gates without sacrificing fidelity. Readers should note, however, that experimental validation on specific hardware platforms will be needed to confirm the predicted robustness under real‑world noise spectra.

High-fidelity quantum gates are a central requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet their implementation is limited by the sensitivity of qubits to environmental noise and by control non-idealities. To mitigate these effects, quantum gates can be designed as dynamically corrected gates (DCGs), where control sequences are engineered to suppress the impact of errors on the resulting operation. Many methods in the literature are able to synthesize DCGs, but they typically rely on numerical optimization, with synthesis times on the order of minutes per gate. Here, we propose an automated semi-analytical method that reduces this cost by orders of magnitude, synthesizing smooth, robust control pulses in tens of milliseconds rather than minutes, with comparable fidelity and robustness. Our approach is based on the Space Curve Quantum Control (SCQC) formalism, where quantum evolution is mapped onto a geometric space curve whose geometric properties determine the target gate and its robustness. We parameterize the curve in the Frenet-Serret frame and employ the Pontryagin Maximum Principle (PMP) to design controls that are robust against both amplitude and dephasing errors. The PMP is formulated as a boundary-value problem and solved using a shooting method. The Frenet-Serret frame is integrated using Rodrigues' formula. Starting from a reference solution, we gradually vary the target rotation angle to construct a library of solutions, whose interpolation provides initial guesses for the shooting parameters of new target gates. We evaluated the method on 2,000 single-qubit rotations, obtaining a mean local optimization time of 39.945 ms per gate after preparation of the interpolation base. Quantum propagation yielded nominal gate infidelities below 10^-9 after virtual phase correction, with verified robustness against quasistatic amplitude and dephasing errors.

item.title: Quantum trajectory of a spin oscillator, continuous retrodiction beyond the Heisenberg uncertainty relation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that by continuously monitoring a macroscopic spin‑oscillator and exploiting information both before and after a given moment, researchers can retrodict the values of non‑commuting quadratures with variances about 1 dB below the conventional Heisenberg limit—a practical realization of quantum smoothing that had previously been limited to theory. The result builds on recent advances in weak continuous measurement and real‑time Bayesian filtering, showing that large atomic ensembles can maintain coherent trajectories for hours while still delivering sub‑standard‑quantum‑limit precision. If integrated into magnetometry or force sensing platforms, such retrodictive estimation could boost sensitivity without requiring exotic squeezed states, though the approach hinges on maintaining low decoherence and high measurement efficiency over long timescales.

The Heisenberg uncertainty relation in quantum mechanics limits the precision of predicting the outcome of measurements of any non-commuting observables. However, this restriction does not apply to retrodictive guessing of the outcomes of past measurements. Here, we experimentally demonstrate this using a spin oscillator consisting of $ 5.17 \times 10^{10}$ rubidium atoms. Through weak continuous measurements, we monitor canonical spin observables $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ with $[\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}},\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}] = i\hbar$. By combining information obtained before and after time $t$, we retrodict the outcomes of measurements of $\hat{x}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\hat{p}_{\mathrm{A}}$ at time $t$ with variances that remain, concurrently over 1.4 hours, $\sim$ 1.01 dB below the bound set by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. We also infer and demonstrate the ability to retrodict, with the same precision, the measurement outcomes for arbitrary quadratures of the spin oscillator. This brings interesting prospects for further research on quantum measurements, and for quantum-enhanced sensing that combines trajectory and entanglement strategies.

item.title: Autler-townes energy-level engineering for high-quality all-microwave qubit gate
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates a clever use of the Autler‑Townes effect to reshape qubit nonlinearity on the fly, allowing an all‑microwave CZ gate that reaches 99.4 % fidelity in just 97 ns without disturbing the computational subspace or shortening coherence times. By sidestepping flux‑tuning and the speed‑leakage trade‑off that have hampered previous microwave‑only schemes, the work offers a simpler hardware topology that can be transplanted to other superconducting platforms and potentially to emerging qubit modalities. The error budget shows static decoherence as the dominant source, suggesting that further gains are realistic once material and environmental noise are reduced.

High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for realizing large-scale fault-tolerant superconducting quantum computing, yet existing approaches are limited: frequency-tuning techniques induce decoherence, while all-microwave-driven schemes suffer the trade-off between gate speed and leakage rate. Here, we introduce an energy-level engineering technique that employs the Autler-Townes effect to manipulate the nonlinearity of qubits without perturbing the computational subspace or degrading coherence time. This approach enables an experimentally validated, fast (97 ns) and high-fidelity (99.40(9)%) CZ gate, where error analysis reveals that gate errors arise mainly from static decoherence. The scheme facilitates fast, high-quality all-microwave gate operations with a simple topology and can be applied across various quantum platforms.

item.title: Monopoles, Scattering and Generalized Symmetries on a Quantum Computer
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that today’s trapped‑ion hardware can move beyond textbook simulations and actually generate the exotic non‑local excitations that underpin recent theoretical breakthroughs in generalized symmetries and duality defects. By engineering a localized quasiparticle wavepacket and then converting it into a string‑like excitation on Quantinuum’s H2 processor, the authors provide the first experimental foothold for studying magnetic‑monopole scattering analogues in spin chains—a problem that has only been resolved analytically in the past year. The work demonstrates a practical protocol that could be repurposed to probe symmetry‑protected topological phases and other many‑body phenomena, although scaling to larger lattices will still depend on further improvements in gate fidelity and error mitigation.

Quantum computers have advanced to the stage that interesting many-body quantum phenomena can be observed. A striking example is the magnetic monopole paradox, a problem that was only solved recently using the language of generalized symmetries. Here we demonstrate a quantum spin chain analogue of magnetic monopole scattering on Quantinuum System Model H2. We implement a novel protocol for preparing a localized quasiparticle wavepacket on top of the ground state. By combining this protocol with time evolution across a duality defect, we efficiently convert local particles into non-local string-like excitations. We demonstrate this particle-to-string conversion in the transverse-field Ising model and a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase of the cluster model. Our results establish duality defects and generalized symmetries as practical resources for preparing and probing non-local excitations on quantum hardware.

item.title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a novel “multi‑robust” pulse design that combines the classic DRAG approach with an iterative quantum Kolmogorov‑Arnold‑Moser (KAM) algorithm, enabling simultaneous suppression of leakage into higher energy levels and resilience to unknown control inhomogeneities. By showing that two‑level robustness can be recovered after only a few KAM iterations and that the resulting pulses are nearly optimal in energy, it offers a practical route to higher‑fidelity gates for transmons and other multi‑level qubits—an advance that dovetails with recent efforts in optimal‑control and error‑mitigation techniques. If experimentally realized, these RDK pulses could reduce calibration overhead and push superconducting processors closer to the fault‑tolerance threshold.

We introduce a multi-robust quantum control strategy designed to suppress multilevel leakage outside the computational qubit space while simultaneously ensuring robustness against unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. It is based on a reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique which allows for the full incorporation of control pulses originally designed for two-level models by using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. We apply it for optimal robust control designed by inverse optimization (RIO), referred to as RDK pulses. We analyze the performance of RDK pulses on various durations, iterations, and robustness types. We show that the two-level robustness is restored after only a few iterations with an asymptotic exponential approximation (i.e. as a superasymptotic series), even for relatively short pulse durations and that the resulting pulses are near optimal in terms of energy compared to the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace. Such pulses are well suited for superconducting transmons as well as other forms of qubits embedded in a multi-level structure. By effectively reproducing a two-level dynamics within a multi-level system, this approach is versatile thanks to its compatibility with two-level control strategies under conditions (smoothness, duration) that are analyzed.

item.title: Detecting Nonbilocal Correlations via Parameterized Elegant Joint Measurement
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how a tunable three‑parameter elegant joint measurement can be used to amplify nonbilocal correlations in a simple two‑source entanglement‑swapping network, providing the first analytic recipe for continuously steering the strength of network‑level quantum effects. By linking the measurement’s entanglement parameter θ directly to the violation of classical bilocal constraints, it bridges recent theoretical advances on network nonlocality with experimentally realistic setups that could improve device‑independent sensing and distributed quantum protocols. The work also highlights that while the scheme is readily implementable with current photonic platforms, scaling to larger networks will still require careful source independence and loss mitigation.

Quantum networks constitute a defining resource for quantum information processing; however, their nonclassical behavior is jointly governed by the choice of measurement basis and the independence of the distributed sources. We study a bilocal entanglement-swapping network in which the central node performs a three-parameter elegant joint measurement (EJM). For two independent Bell-state sources, we construct two binary edge observables and then derive a quantum prediction involving three parameters, which surpasses the classical constraints. In particular, the parameter θ controls both the degree of entanglement of the EJM basis states and the maximum value of the quantum prediction. These results provide an analytic and directly reproducible route for tuning nonbilocal correlations in an experimentally relevant two-source network.

item.title: Separability and lower bounds of concurrence via symmetric measurement correlations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces experimentally friendly separability tests that rely only on symmetric measurement‑correlation matrices, sidestepping full state tomography—a major bottleneck for scaling up entanglement verification in near‑term quantum devices and sensing platforms. By turning the same data into tighter lower bounds on concurrence, the authors provide a practical way to quantify entanglement strength, improving on several recent criteria that have been adopted in photonic and superconducting experiments. The results could streamline real‑time monitoring of multipartite resources in quantum sensors, though their performance still depends on the ability to implement the required symmetric measurement settings with low noise.

The detection and quantification of quantum entanglement is a central issue in quantum information science, particularly for unknown quantum states. Based on symmetric measurement correlation matrices, we present a family of separability criteria that can be experimentally applied without state tomography, and recover some related existing criteria as special cases. Using the constructed correlation matrices, we further derive a class of lower bounds of concurrence. Through illustrative examples, we demonstrate that our criteria outperform some existing separability criteria in entanglement detection, and that the obtained lower bounds on concurrence are tighter than known counterparts.

item.title: Arithmetic Depth, Minimal Gate Alphabets, and Exact Program-State Resources for Single-Qubit Dyadic Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that for the entire family of single‑qubit “dyadic” rotations—those built from angles π/2^D—the deepest layer of exact resources can be identified analytically rather than bounded conservatively, collapsing gate count, field extension depth and program‑state complexity into a single minimal value. By proving a descent theorem that ties the Clifford‑cyclotomic tower to real cyclotomic fields, the authors give a rigorous certificate for optimal synthesis that complements recent advances in Clifford + T and other fixed‑alphabet compilers, promising tighter control of gate overhead on near‑term hardware where every non‑Clifford operation is costly. The result could streamline compiler pipelines and error‑budget calculations, though its current scope is limited to single‑qubit dyadic programs and will need extension before impacting multi‑qubit algorithm design.

Resource analyses for quantum programs commonly provide safe upper bounds on qubits, gates, or non-Clifford operations. We study a single-qubit dyadic fragment in which the deepest exact resource layer can instead be inferred exactly. Starting from the normalized-midpoint misty-state syntax, we define dyadic program states and the real cyclotomic tower $K_D=\mathbb Q(2\cos(π/2^D))$. For the projective single-qubit Clifford-cyclotomic tower $\widehat G_D\subseteq SO(3)$, we prove the relative intersection law $\widehat G_D\cap SO(3,K_d)=\widehat G_d$ for $d\le D$. Combining this descent theorem with an arithmetic-closure invariant for adaptive stabilizer processing yields $\mathrm{Fdepth}(U)=\mathrm{Adepth}(U)=\mathrm{Rdepth}(U)$: the smallest real cyclotomic field containing the Bloch matrix of an exactly synthesizable channel, the shallowest dyadic gate alphabet realizing it up to global phase, and the shallowest dyadic program-state layer sufficient for exact stabilizer-assisted implementation coincide. At that common minimum, known fixed-alphabet synthesis gives minimum primitive-rotation count. We package the result as an exact static resource effect and outline a certificate-producing compiler.

item.title: Optimal Holding Times for Entanglement Swapping
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles a bottleneck in long‑distance quantum networking by showing how to set optimal memory holding times for heterogeneous repeater links, directly boosting the rate at which high‑fidelity entanglement can be swapped across a chain. By integrating realistic decoherence rates, multi‑memory capacities and classical latency into analytical throughput models, the work bridges the gap between abstract protocol design and the engineering constraints that recent fiber‑based and satellite QKD demonstrations are confronting. The resulting guidelines could help network architects tune hardware parameters to meet strict fidelity targets without over‑provisioning resources, though the benefits will depend on the specific memory technologies and link asymmetries in a given deployment.

We revisit the optimization of entanglement holding times in memory-based quantum repeaters for maximizing entanglement swapping throughput under different fidelity constraints - strict, probabilistic, and mean. We consider two heterogeneous quantum links that are equipped with single or multiple memories and differ in decoherence rates, memory capacities, entanglement attempt rates and success probabilities, as well as classical communication latencies. Efficient models are developed to estimate the expected entanglement throughput and the probability density functions of the conditional wait time to swap. The models are then used to satisfy different fidelity requirements by optimizing the maximum holding times for the two links. Finally, our proposed model and approach are validated with a discrete-event quantum network simulator.

item.title: Resource-efficient formulations of the Knapsack problem for quantum computing
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the way a combinatorial problem is encoded for quantum hardware can be as important as the algorithm itself, demonstrating that more compact QUBO formulations of the classic Knapsack problem dramatically boost success rates on both LR‑QAOA simulations and D‑Wave annealers. By cutting slack variables or tightening penalty constants, the authors achieve several orders of magnitude higher optimal‑solution probabilities, a result that directly addresses one of the biggest bottlenecks—excess qubit overhead—in near‑term quantum optimization. The work therefore provides a practical template for other inequality‑constrained problems, suggesting that smarter encodings could unlock better performance from today’s noisy intermediate‑scale quantum devices.

Quantum computing has emerged as a new tool for solving combinatorial optimization problems. Quantum optimization approaches usually operate on the subclass of Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problems. Many optimization problems can be reformulated in this form, though there are often multiple ways to do so. The choice of formulation can considerably affect the performance of QUBO solvers in practice. In this work, we study QUBO formulations of the Knapsack problem, a canonical example of a problem with inequality constraints. In the standard formulation these constraints are converted into penalty terms, which requires additional slack variables. Here, we investigate three more resource-efficient approaches for formulating the Knapsack as a QUBO. The first two modify the standard formulation, either by deriving a smaller penalty constant or by reducing the number of slack variables. The third approach is a wholly different method, which avoids the use of slack variables entirely. All three approaches increase the probability of finding the optimal solution, both in simulations of the linear ramp Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (LR-QAOA) and on a D-Wave quantum annealer. The slackless method performs best, increasing success probabilities by several orders of magnitude even for relatively small problem sizes.

item.title: Solving a non-abelian hidden subgroup problem on a trapped-ion quantum computer: the power of the measurement basis
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks the first experimental realization of a non‑abelian hidden subgroup problem on a trapped‑ion processor, confirming that the choice of measurement basis—not just circuit depth—can be the decisive factor for quantum speed‑ups in problems such as graph isomorphism and lattice‑based cryptography. By testing weak, strong (adapted), adjacent‑pair, and forgetful sampling strategies on the IonQ Forte device, the authors show that theoretical predictions about when information can be extracted survive realistic noise levels, and even surpass an optimally tuned classical algorithm for a three‑query instance. The work demonstrates a concrete pathway toward quantum algorithms that exploit group structure beyond the abelian case, while reminding readers that scaling to larger groups will still demand improvements in qubit count and error rates.

The hidden subgroup problem (HSP) unifies many of the best-known quantum speed-ups. For abelian groups it is solved efficiently by weak Fourier sampling, but for non-abelian groups, which include the cases relevant to graph isomorphism and lattice-based cryptography, the right measurement basis is crucial and often unknown. We experimentally study the HSP over the $q$-hedral groups $\mathbb{Z}_q \ltimes \mathbb{Z}_p$, which interpolate between the dihedral and affine groups and mark a boundary between instances that are efficiently solvable and those that are only information-theoretically solvable. On the IonQ Forte trapped-ion quantum computer, with $p \le 7$, we implement weak Fourier sampling, strong Fourier sampling in an adapted basis, strong Fourier sampling of adjacent pairs, and forgetful abelian sampling. We demonstrate that the theoretical predictions of Moore, Rockmore, Russell and Schulman survive on a noisy device: weak sampling reveals nothing about the hidden subgroup, the adapted basis succeeds for large $q$, adjacent pairs succeed for small $q$, and forgetful sampling saturates below unit success. For $p=7$, $q=6$, the hardware exceeds the success probability of an exhaustively optimised classical algorithm for up to three oracle queries.

item.title: QASPA-MaxCut on Unweighted Graphs: Edge Encoding and QAOA Restarts
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces QASPA‑MaxCut, a novel edge‑encoding circuit that replaces the standard QAOA mixer with controlled R_y rotations and shows how a simple one‑layer ansatz can already match or exceed depth‑one QAOA on small unweighted graphs. By analytically deriving the two‑qubit algebra and demonstrating systematic gains through classical restarts, the work provides a concrete blueprint for low‑depth variational algorithms that are easier to implement on noisy hardware. Max-Cut is a common testbed for near-term quantum optimization because it has a simple Ising Hamiltonian, established classical baselines, and a parameterized quantum circuit whose performance depends on the outer classical optimizer. This paper develops QASPA-MaxCut, a shift-phase circuit for Max-Cut that encodes graph edges through controlled $R_y$ rotations of the form $\mathrm{CX}_{ij}R_y(θ_{ij})\mathrm{CX}_{ij}$. We derive the exact two-qubit algebra of the edge block, trace an unweighted four-vertex example, and compare one-layer QASPA-MaxCut with depth-one QAOA by exact state-vector simulation. The protocol uses seed 42, evaluates connected backbone-augmented random graphs with additional-edge probabilities $p_{\mathrm{edge}}\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7\}$, and adds nineteen custom unweighted topologies. The QASPA-MaxCut score is reported after the algorithm's classical selection stage: the four leading QASPA bit strings are evaluated by the Max-Cut objective, and the best cut is retained. The QAOA score is the expected approximation ratio after local optimization, reported as a best-of-$k$ curve over one to ten restarts. In these small exact simulations, fixed-angle QASPA-MaxCut produces reported group-mean selection ratios between $0.955$ and $1.000$, the topology-level readout is unchanged in the retained finite-shot checks under the rule $\lceil 0.03047\cdot 2^n+1016.2\rceil$, and depth-one QAOA improves with additional classical restarts while remaining lower than the QASPA selection score in the reported mean summaries. This comparison motivates further study of the classical search budget needed to obtain competitive Max-Cut samples at shallow circuit depth.

item.title: First-principles study of the formation of Group-IV--vacancy color centers in diamond
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pinpoints why the promising group‑IV–vacancy (SiV, GeV, SnV, PbV) color centers often appear at far lower concentrations than ion‑implantation doses would suggest: competing capture of carbon interstitials or extra vacancies readily converts the split‑vacancy configuration into less useful defects. By quantifying binding energies, diffusion barriers and charge transition levels with first‑principles calculations, the authors show that controlling the Fermi level during annealing could suppress these side reactions and boost the yield of optically active spin qubits. The insight dovetails with recent experimental pushes to engineer high‑purity diamond platforms for quantum networking, offering a concrete materials‑science lever to improve device reproducibility.

$XV$ ($X$ is Si, Ge, Sn, or Pb, and $V$ is the carbon vacancy) color centers are promising platforms for quantum computing and quantum information science due to their favorable optical and spin properties. They are commonly fabricated by ion implantation, which inevitably introduces vacancies and carbon self-interstitials (C$_i$) into the lattice. However, the microscopic formation mechanism remains unclear, limiting the yield and stability of $XV$ centers. Here, first-principles calculations are conducted to systematically investigate the roles of $V$ and C$_i$ in $XV$ formation. We find that $XV$ formation is energetically favorable, with large binding energies and low diffusion barriers. Nevertheless, $XV$ readily captures C$_i$ to form substitutional defect $X_s$, or captures an additional $V$ to form the complex $XV_2$. Charge transition levels show that oppositely charged reactants never meet in these reactions, and that Coulomb repulsion blocks them only when both reactants carry charges of the same sign, which for the capture of C$_i$ requires strongly n- or p-type conditions. These competing defect reactions destabilize the split-vacancy configuration and could account for the low formation yield of $XV$ centers, so that they appear at concentrations well below those expected from the implanted dose. Our results elucidate the microscopic origin of this intrinsic instability and suggest that Fermi-level control may suppress defect conversions and stabilize the split-vacancy configuration.

item.title: Flux Crosstalk Calibration from Zero Knowledge to High Precision in Fully Tunable Superconducting Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles one of the thorniest bottlenecks for scaling superconducting quantum processors—flux‑crosstalk between tunable qubits and couplers—by introducing calibration techniques that work without any prior spectroscopy or dedicated readout lines. By leveraging intrinsic coupler‑resonator interactions, the zero‑knowledge method speeds up chip bring‑up, while the symmetric branch cancellation scheme pushes residual crosstalk down to below 5 × 10⁻⁵, a precision level needed for error‑corrected operation. Together they give hardware teams a practical pathway from initial device turn‑on to the fine‑grained control required for large‑scale, fully tunable architectures.

Precise and independent flux control is essential for scalable superconducting processors built from frequency-tunable qubits and couplers, but flux crosstalk undermines it. Conventional calibration methods rely either on dedicated readout channels, which tunable couplers typically lack, or on readout schemes requiring extensive prior spectroscopy of the qubit and coupler. We demonstrate two independent methods that characterize coupler flux crosstalk without directly driving or measuring the couplers. The first method is zero-knowledge characterization, which exploits intrinsic coupler-resonator coupling to yield rapid and accurate estimates with no prior qubit or coupler spectroscopy, accelerating large scale bring-up. The second method is symmetric branch cancellation, which isolates crosstalk from other dispersive effects allowing for quantifying with high precision. Combined with an improved iterative procedure, these methods suppress residual coupler crosstalk below $5\times10^{-5}$, providing a complete route from zero-knowledge initialization to high-precision crosstalk characterization in fully tunable architectures.

item.title: Efficient quantum ultraspherical transform and a well-conditioned quantum spectral method
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first fully efficient quantum circuit for ultraspherical transforms beyond the cosine‑ and sine‑case, showing that a polynomial‑in‑log N gate count suffices to switch between pointwise amplitudes and spectral coefficients for any fixed integer order m≥2. By coupling this transform with a well‑conditioned preconditioning strategy, the authors construct a quantum spectral solver whose linear‑system condition numbers remain bounded, extending recent quantum linear‑equation algorithms into the realm of high‑accuracy differential‑equation simulation. The result narrows a key practical gap—efficiently preparing and manipulating smooth function representations on a quantum computer—bringing hardware‑friendly quantum PDE solvers one step closer to real‑world applications.

Solving differential equations is a promising application of quantum computing. Spectral methods, where the solution is represented by coefficients in a basis, are particularly well suited to quantum solvers because their structured discretizations can enable efficient linear-algebra operations while providing rapid convergence. Their quantum implementation, however, requires an efficient transform between amplitudes encoding function values and amplitudes encoding expansion coefficients. This work develops two key components of a quantum spectral method. First, we construct the quantum ultraspherical transform (QUT) for orthonormal ultraspherical polynomials, a basis that supports sparse and well-conditioned discretizations of differential equations. For the basis parameters $m=0$ and $1$, this transform reduces to the discrete cosine and sine transforms with known efficient circuits. Our contribution covers every fixed integer $m\geq2$: for dimensions $N$ with $N+m=2^n$, where $n$ is the number of qubits, the QUT achieves error at most $\varepsilon$ using a gate count polynomial in $n$ and $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. The construction builds on the quantum Fourier transform, augmented by approximations whose accuracy guarantees are independent of $N$. Second, we develop a quantum spectral solver for regular linear ordinary differential equations based on the QUT. Under suitable boundary conditions and data-access assumptions, preconditioning keeps condition numbers bounded independently of the basis size, allowing the solution state to be prepared at polylogarithmic cost in system size and inverse error. Together, these contributions provide a framework for quantum spectral methods with the potential to solve linear differential equations efficiently.

item.title: Parrondo's paradox for three discrete-time quantum walks with distinct shift operators
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article expands the toolbox for discrete‑time quantum walks by showing that Parrondo’s paradox can be realized with a single coin but three distinct shift operators, opening a new route to engineer counterintuitive transport behavior without complex coin sequences. By linking the paradox to the evolution of walker–coin entanglement, it provides fresh insight into how bias reversal can be harnessed for dynamic control in quantum algorithms and simulation protocols. The work also highlights that richer shift dynamics—beyond simple left/right moves—may become a practical lever for designing more versatile quantum walk‑based processors, though experimental implementation will need to address the added hardware complexity of multi‑outcome shifts.

Parrondo's paradox describes a surprising phenomenon in which certain combinations of biased quantum walks result in an unexpected reversal of their bias direction. To date, research on this effect has predominantly focused on one-dimensional discrete-time quantum walks that employ fixed sequences of two or three quantum coins, paired with a single shift operator. In this work, we first introduce a wide class of unitary shift operators which allow for three movement options (left, right or stay in place) of a walker in one time step, and we then demonstrate that Parrondo's paradox can also arise with a single coin and three distinct shift operators. Furthermore, we investigate how this paradox influences the time evolution of quantum entanglement between the walker and the coin in such quantum walks.
